title: Governor of Oregon

context.text: Incumbent Democrat Tina Kotek is seeking a second term and won her party's May 19 primary with 84 percent of the vote. State Sen. Christine Drazan, the 2022 Republican nominee, won the Republican primary with 41 percent in a crowded field. It is Oregon's first gubernatorial rematch since 1978.

Kotek was also cross-nominated by the Oregon Working Families Party in August; the Libertarian Party of Oregon cross-nominated Drazan in late July, the first time in 40 years the party has not fielded its own gubernatorial candidate. Pacific Green Party nominee Brett Smith is the only other candidate; the Independent Party of Oregon, Progressive Party and No Labels Party made no nomination.

candidates.name: Tina Kotek
candidates.ballotNote: Won the Democratic primary with 84% of the vote; cross-nominated by the Working Families Party.

priorities.text: Reducing unsheltered homelessness through emergency orders and a permanent statewide shelter program.
Increasing housing supply by cutting red tape and funding infrastructure and affordable housing.
Preserving the Oregon Health Plan and the state's Medicaid system from federal cuts.

Per a joint statement with the Working Families Party, committed to pursue statewide universal preschool, protect farmworker overtime and climate protection policies, and defend the state's sanctuary laws.

positions.summary: Commemorated the July 2025 signing of bills aimed at speeding middle-housing production and funding housing infrastructure, saying 'we have to cut red tape and get out of our own way.'
Committed, in exchange for the Working Families Party cross-nomination, to pursue statewide universal preschool modeled on Multnomah County's Preschool For All.
Agreed, in a joint statement with the Working Families Party, to defend Oregon's sanctuary laws.

Said in the October 13 debate she is trying to preserve the state's Medicaid system from cuts under the Trump administration, and criticized Drazan's vote against a tax package funding the Oregon Health Plan.

record.text: Commemorated the signing of House Bill 3644, which creates an ongoing statewide shelter program and includes $204.9 million for the next two years.

Commemorated the signing of House Bill 2138, House Bill 3031, House Bill 2258, Senate Bill 684 and House Bill 3145, bipartisan bills on housing construction, including middle-housing production and a Housing Infrastructure Project Fund.

Extended the statewide homelessness emergency by Executive Order 25-01, which directs state agencies to continue reducing the number of people experiencing homelessness; the emergency was first declared on January 10, 2023.

candidates.name: Christine Drazan
candidates.ballotNote: Won the Republican primary with 41% of the vote; cross-nominated by the Libertarian Party of Oregon. Republican nominee for governor in 2022.

priorities.text: Cutting taxes, speeding permitting and growing the economy.
Overhauling Oregon's land-use laws and cutting building regulations to increase housing.

Directing people experiencing homelessness into detox, treatment and long-term recovery; at the October 13 debate she said that movement, not the provision of housing alone, should be the measure of success.

positions.summary: Has described herself as pro-life; in a 2022 interview said she would veto a bill to expand abortion access but did not plan to push new limits in a Democratic-controlled legislature. This statement is from her 2022 campaign; a 2026 statement was not found.
positions.quote: I am in fact a pro-life woman.

positions.summary: Pledged in the October 13 debate to cut building regulations and overhaul Oregon's land-use laws.

record.text: Voted no on House Bill 4088, a bill declaring state policy to protect reproductive and gender-affirming health care activities, which passed the Senate 18–12.
Voted no on House Bill 4127, requiring the Oregon Health Authority to pay certain nonprofit reproductive health providers with state funds, which passed the Senate 18–11.
Voted no on House Bill 4134, which increases the state transient lodging tax and passed the Senate 20–9.
Said she voted against a tax package that funds the Oregon Health Plan because it enacted new taxes.

candidates.name: Brett Smith
candidates.ballotNote: Nominee of the Pacific Green Party; won the party's nomination over three other candidates.

priorities.text: Says he opposes war and corruption, as do the Libertarian and Pacific Green parties he considered running with.
Corruption, which he calls the single most important issue facing the state.
Affordability, including a surcharge on large employers paying below a living wage and a universal public health option.

positions.summary: Proposes opening the Oregon Health Plan to all Oregon residents regardless of income.
positions.quote: Expand eligibility for the Oregon Health Plan to all Oregon residents, regardless of income, employment status, or preexisting conditions.

statements.quote: A single adult working full time in Oregon needs $26.46 an hour to cover basic needs without public assistance, and Oregon's minimum wage falls short of that figure by as much as $12 an hour in nonurban counties.
statements.context: On his campaign website, introducing a proposed surcharge on employers with 50 or more employees

statements.quote: It's a war. It's unconstitutional. It hasn't been sanctioned by Congress.
statements.context: In a 'Meet the Candidate' interview with KEPW 97.3, Aug. 2026, about the current U.S. war

candidates.researchNotes: Positions and statements come from his campaign website (brett-smith.us) and a KEPW 97.3 'Meet the Candidate' interview. No abortion, gun, immigration or other positions found; in the interview he calls these 'real issues' without stating positions.

researchNotes: Ballotpedia was blocked in this environment and the Oregon Secretary of State's certified candidate list could not be loaded (the Elections Division pages did not expose it), so the slate is a news-only check: OPB (July 23, August 21, September 16) reports Kotek, Drazan and Pacific Green's Brett Smith as the only names on the ballot, consistent with Wikipedia. Oregon elects its governor alone (no running mates). Drazan's 2026 stated positions are thinly sourced: her abortion statement dates from 2022, and her campaign website could not be loaded. Brett Smith has little public footprint; his profile rests on OPB reporting only (an earlier version relied on The Ballot Brief, which says its content is AI-assisted, and was removed, including its claims about his campaign priorities and Voters' Pamphlet statement). Drazan's roll-call votes were checked against the Oregon Legislature's official OData vote feed (2026 session only). No Oregon official record page for Kotek's 2023-2024 actions beyond those listed was reviewed.
